episode_title: Adam Mosseri: AI is a tailwind for authenticity
description_html:
Adam Mosseri is the Head of Instagram, where he oversees an app used by over 3 billion people. He also leads the team building Threads. Adam has run Instagram for longer than its founders did, after taking over from Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger in 2018. A designer by training, he spent over 15 years at Meta, starting as a designer on Facebook’s mobile app, rising to lead Facebook’s News Feed, and eventually chosen to lead Instagram. During his tenure, Instagram’s user base has more than tripled.

In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:

1. How the canonical product team structure is changing in 2026, from baker’s-dozen specialist teams to lean pods of four to six generalists

2. The rise of the “product staff” role—a blending of PM, design, data science, and research into one generalist operator

3. Why Adam is bullish on designers even as functional boundaries dissolve, and which roles are most at risk

4. What the Instagram algorithm knows about you, and why it’s only now catching up to what people assumed it knew years ago

5. Why the rise of AI-generated content is a tailwind for Instagram, and how the company is thinking about creator identity in a synthetic-content world

6. The two biggest product failures of Adam’s career—Facebook Home and the first version of Reels

summary.overview: Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram, discusses how AI is changing product teams, hiring, software development, and the role of human judgment. He also explains Instagram’s approach to recommendation algorithms, AI-generated content, creator discovery, platform controversies, and raising children with technology.

takeaways.heading: Product teams are getting smaller and more generalist
takeaways.detail: Instagram is moving from traditional teams of roughly a dozen specialists to “pods” of around six or seven people: four to six more-generalist engineers, a “product staff” lead, and specialists brought in when needed. Fewer people coordinating can lead to faster decisions and less “design by committee.”

takeaways.heading: The product staff role blends functions
takeaways.detail: Product staff members may handle parts of product management, design, research, and data science, using internal tools to automate mechanical work such as waterfall analysis. Specialists remain important for novel design, advanced research, or complex data-science problems.

takeaways.heading: Taste and design matter more when building gets easier
takeaways.detail: Adam said product taste is increasingly valuable because teams must spend more time deciding what to build, not merely building it. He is optimistic about designers because they often bring taste that is difficult to automate, though some designers and data scientists may move into broader product-staff roles.

takeaways.heading: AI is blurring career paths, but specialists will remain
takeaways.detail: Functional boundaries will continue to weaken, and less-senior specialists may move into generalist roles. Adam still expects companies to hire and mentor future senior specialists rather than relying only on today’s experts.

takeaways.heading: Traits he looks for in people include grit, fast learning, and self-awareness
takeaways.detail: In the current environment, he also emphasizes curiosity and willingness to try things, make mistakes, and “sound like an idiot” while learning. He expects fewer roles managing thousands of people as teams become smaller, though large-scale organizational leadership will remain a distinct skill.

takeaways.heading: AI is changing who can be effective
takeaways.detail: Engineers now spend more time planning and reviewing code than writing it; designers can program, engineers can analyze data, and data scientists can help develop designs. Adam stressed that AI tools are “not binary”: they are excellent at some tasks and remarkably bad at others, so people need judgment about both their current and likely future capabilities.

takeaways.heading: Human value will increasingly center on taste, judgment, vision, and strategy
takeaways.detail: Adam described vision as the desired state of the product or world, and strategy as an opinionated path toward it—something a reasonable person should be able to disagree with. AI can help with strategy when given detailed constraints and critical feedback, but a generic prompt tends to produce predictable answers.

takeaways.heading: Product leaders are often curators rather than idea machines
takeaways.detail: The strongest leaders curate people, ideas, technologies, and strategies, creating an environment where good ideas emerge and are selected. They also build complementary leadership teams with trust, rapport, and a good working “vibe.”

takeaways.heading: Instagram’s algorithm is less semantically sophisticated than many assume
takeaways.detail: Historically, it often relied on large embedding models and correlations rather than explicitly knowing that someone likes a topic such as surfing. Instagram is now using LLMs to describe otherwise unreadable patterns in its embedding space through a feature called “Your Algorithm,” which lets users view and adjust topics they are believed to like.

takeaways.heading: Chronological feeds involve trade-offs
takeaways.detail: Adam said a purely chronological feed can favor publishers and professional accounts that post constantly, while burying occasional posts from friends. Recency matters, but it is not the only measure of relevance; Instagram’s surveys suggest that chronological feeds reduce both usage and overall satisfaction over time.

takeaways.heading: AI-generated content could be a tailwind for Instagram, but ranking it will be difficult
takeaways.detail: Adam expects people to seek out creativity, authenticity, and the individuals behind content in a world with abundant synthetic media. Instagram does not intend to automatically filter AI content; instead, it wants to identify or label it, while acknowledging that detection may become unreliable as models improve.

takeaways.heading: Creators and exploration-based recommendations are central to Instagram’s strategy
takeaways.detail: Adam said Instagram is investing in individuals broadly—including journalists, artists, and small businesses—and learning from TikTok’s ability to help niche and emerging creators find audiences. Instagram is trying to optimize not only for engagement but also originality, recency, and the number of pieces of content that break out.

takeaways.heading: Adam embraces public criticism of Instagram
takeaways.detail: He began speaking openly about Facebook’s News Feed because the debate was happening anyway, and he believed the company should explain its decisions and trade-offs. He sees accessibility and authenticity as ways to reduce fear of systems people do not understand, though criticism can still be personally difficult.

takeaways.heading: Instagram’s controversial video-feed moment involved several issues at once
takeaways.detail: A test shown to a small percentage of iOS users was conflated with increased Reels recommendations, more content from accounts users did not follow, and creator concerns about reach. Adam said Instagram had pushed too quickly, but still believes continued evolution—including video, DMs, Stories, ranking, and recommendations—is necessary.

takeaways.heading: Two failures shaped Adam’s career
takeaways.detail: Facebook Home, an Android-based operating-system and hardware project, was a “spectacular failure” that taught him about carriers, OEMs, certification, and operating systems. He also believes Instagram’s first Reels implementation, built on top of Stories, was a mistake that delayed a stronger standalone product.

takeaways.heading: For his children, Adam favors boundaries plus AI literacy
takeaways.detail: His children, ages 10, 8, and 6, earn limited iPad time, and he approves the apps they use. He supports no phones in classrooms but also wants children to learn how to use AI, so he has begun “vibe coding” a video game with his 10-year-old using Claude Code.

quotes.text: In a world where it’s easier to build things, it’s more important to make sure that your time is spent figuring out what you should be building in the first place.
The people who I think are going to make the most of it are the ones who are clear-eyed about what AI is good at and what it’s not good at.
I don’t think we should judge content based on the tool that made it.
